topics.title: Python (programming language)
topics.summary: Python is a high-level, interpreted, dynamically typed language designed for readability. Created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991, it uses indentation to define blocks and ships a very large standard library.

sections.heading: Core idea
sections.text: Python optimises for human reading time rather than machine execution time. Statements end at a newline, blocks are marked by indentation instead of braces, and almost everything is an object with a runtime type. The interpreter compiles source to bytecode, which the Python virtual machine executes.

sections.heading: How it works in practice
sections.text: You write a .py file, the interpreter tokenises and parses it into an AST, compiles it to bytecode, then runs it. Packages are installed into an environment with pip. Because it is interpreted, iteration is fast; because it is dynamic, most errors surface at runtime, which is why tests and type hints matter.

sections.heading: Where it is used
sections.text: Automation and scripting, web backends (Django, FastAPI, Flask), data science (pandas, NumPy), machine learning (PyTorch, scikit-learn), and glue code around APIs. It is also the most common language for teaching programming and for building AI agents.

topics.example: A list comprehension turns a loop into one readable line: squares = [n*n for n in range(5)] produces [0, 1, 4, 9, 16].

topics.title: Artificial intelligence
topics.summary: AI is the field of building systems that perform tasks associated with human intelligence: perceiving, reasoning, planning, learning, generating language and acting toward goals.

sections.heading: Two eras
sections.text: Symbolic AI (1950s-1980s) encoded expert knowledge as explicit rules and logic. Modern AI is predominantly statistical: models learn parameters from data. The 2012 deep-learning breakthrough in image recognition, driven by GPUs and large datasets, shifted the field toward neural networks.

sections.heading: What it is not
sections.text: Today's systems are narrow: a model that plays chess cannot drive a car. They do not possess consciousness, intentions or understanding in the human sense. They are extremely good at learning statistical structure in their training distribution and much weaker outside it.

sections.heading: Main branches
sections.text: Machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, computer vision, robotics, planning and search, and reinforcement learning. Generative AI is the subset that produces new text, images, audio or code rather than just classifying or predicting.

topics.example: A spam filter learns from thousands of labelled emails instead of a human hand-writing every rule.

topics.title: Machine learning
topics.summary: Machine learning is the subset of AI where a program improves at a task by fitting parameters to examples, rather than being explicitly programmed with rules.

sections.heading: The training loop
sections.text: Choose a model with adjustable parameters, define a loss function that measures how wrong its predictions are, then use gradient descent and backpropagation to adjust parameters so the loss falls. Repeat over many batches of data until validation performance stops improving.

sections.heading: Three paradigms
sections.text: Supervised learning uses labelled input-output pairs (classification, regression). Unsupervised learning finds structure without labels (clustering, dimensionality reduction). Reinforcement learning learns by receiving rewards from an environment.

sections.heading: Why models fail
sections.text: Overfitting memorises training data and generalises poorly; underfitting never captures the pattern; data leakage lets a model cheat by seeing the answer; distribution shift makes a model degrade when the real world changes. Regularisation, held-out test sets and monitoring address these.

topics.example: Predicting house prices from size, location and age is a regression task; judging whether an email is spam is classification.

topics.title: Large language model (LLM)
topics.summary: An LLM is a large neural network, usually a Transformer, trained to predict the next token in a sequence. That one objective, applied at scale, produces abilities like summarising, translating, coding and multi-step reasoning.

sections.heading: Architecture
sections.text: Transformers use self-attention, which lets every token weigh every other token in its context window. Stacking attention and feed-forward layers with residual connections produces a model with billions of parameters. The context window bounds how much text it can consider at once.

sections.heading: From pretraining to assistant
sections.text: Pretraining on vast text corpora teaches language patterns. Instruction tuning on prompt-response pairs and RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback) then shape the model into a helpful assistant. A system prompt sets its behaviour at inference time.

sections.heading: Known limits
sections.text: LLMs do not look up facts in a database: they generate plausible continuations, which causes hallucination. They are weak at exact arithmetic, cannot see events after their training cutoff, and their outputs are sensitive to phrasing. Tools, retrieval and grounding mitigate these.

topics.example: Asking a model '2^10 + sqrt(81)' may produce a confident wrong number; giving it a calculator tool makes it exact.

topics.title: Neural networks and deep learning
topics.summary: A neural network is a stack of layers that apply weighted sums followed by non-linear activation functions. Depth lets it build increasingly abstract representations of the input.

sections.heading: Forward pass
sections.text: Each neuron computes z = w.x + b then applies an activation such as ReLU, sigmoid or GELU. Stacking layers means early layers detect simple features (edges, word pieces) and later layers combine them into concepts (shapes, sentences, objects).

sections.heading: Learning
sections.text: A loss compares prediction to target. Backpropagation applies the chain rule to compute the gradient of that loss with respect to every weight, and an optimiser such as Adam takes a small step downhill. Batches, learning-rate schedules and normalisation keep training stable.

sections.heading: Common architectures
sections.text: CNNs for images with shared convolutional filters, RNNs and LSTMs for sequences (largely superseded), Transformers for language and vision, and autoencoders/diffusion models for generation.

topics.example: In an image model, layer 1 sees edges, layer 3 sees corners and textures, layer 10 sees eyes and wheels.

topics.title: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
topics.summary: RAG gives a language model relevant documents at answer time: retrieve passages from a knowledge store, insert them into the prompt, and ask the model to answer using them with citations.

sections.heading: Pipeline
sections.text: Ingest documents and split them into chunks, embed or index each chunk, then at query time rank chunks by relevance (BM25 keyword search, dense vector similarity, or both). Top passages are placed in the prompt as context, and the model is instructed to ground its answer in them.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: It reduces hallucination, lets you update knowledge without retraining, enables private or domain-specific data, and makes answers auditable through citations. It is the standard pattern behind 'chat with your documents' products.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.text: Bad chunking loses context; poor retrieval returns irrelevant passages; the model may ignore the context; stale indexes give outdated facts. Hybrid search, reranking, query rewriting and evaluation sets are typical fixes.

topics.example: Ryzek AI uses BM25 over its curated knowledge base plus cached Wikipedia articles before composing a detailed answer.

topics.title: AI agents and tool use
topics.summary: An AI agent is a language model inside a control loop: it observes a request, decides whether to call a tool, reads the result, and repeats until it can answer. The loop, not the model, is what makes it an agent.

sections.heading: The loop
sections.text: Plan (or react), select a tool with structured arguments, execute it, append the observation to the conversation, and continue. Frameworks such as ReAct interleave reasoning traces with actions. A step budget prevents infinite loops.

sections.heading: Tool design
sections.text: Each tool needs a precise name, a description of when to use it and a JSON schema for arguments. Good tools are narrow, deterministic and return compact strings. Errors should be returned as text so the model can recover rather than crashing the loop.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.text: Prompt injection in retrieved content can hijack the agent; unbounded tool access can cause damage; cost and latency grow with steps. Least-privilege tools, human approval for side effects and strict timeouts are the standard mitigations.

topics.example: Ask 'what is 17% of 240?' and the agent calls calculator('17/100*240'), reads '40.8', then replies.

topics.title: Prompt and context engineering
topics.summary: Prompt engineering is the practice of designing the instructions, examples and context given to a model so its output is reliable, correctly formatted and useful.

sections.heading: Reliable patterns
sections.text: State the role and the rules, specify the output format, give few-shot examples, ask for step-by-step reasoning when useful, and define what to do when information is missing. Constraints should be positive ('always answer, state assumptions') rather than only prohibitions.

sections.heading: Context engineering
sections.text: Beyond the instruction text, you control which history, retrieved documents, tool results and memory enter the context window. Ordering matters, long contexts cost money and can dilute attention, so compact and rank the context you include.

sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.text: Treat prompts like code: keep a fixed test set of inputs, score outputs on accuracy, format and length, and regression-test whenever you change the system prompt or model.

topics.example: Ryzek's system prompt explicitly forbids empty replies and requires headings, assumptions and one clarifying question.

topics.title: APIs and web services
topics.summary: An API is a defined contract that lets one program request work or data from another. Web APIs usually exchange JSON over HTTP.

sections.heading: Anatomy of a call
sections.text: A request has a method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), a URL path, headers (authentication, content type), optional query parameters and a body. The response has a status code, headers and a body. Idempotent methods like GET and PUT are safe to retry.

sections.heading: Design basics
sections.text: Use nouns for resources, version the path (/v1/...), return meaningful status codes, validate input, paginate lists, rate-limit clients, and document errors. Auth is commonly an API key, OAuth token or signed request.

sections.heading: Status codes
sections.text: 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content), 4xx client error (400 bad request, 401 unauthenticated, 403 forbidden, 404 not found, 429 too many requests), 5xx server error (500, 502, 503).

topics.example: POST /api/chat with {'message': 'hi'} returns {'reply': '...'} in Ryzek's own server.

topics.title: HTTP and the web
topics.summary: HTTP is the stateless request/response protocol of the web. HTTPS is HTTP wrapped in TLS encryption, which provides confidentiality, integrity and server identity.

sections.heading: Lifecycle
sections.text: The browser resolves a domain via DNS, opens a TCP connection (and a TLS handshake for HTTPS), sends a request, and reads the response. Cookies and tokens add session state on top of an otherwise stateless protocol.

sections.heading: Important headers
sections.text: Content-Type describes the body, Authorization carries credentials, Cache-Control governs caching, and CORS headers (Access-Control-Allow-Origin) control which browser origins may read a cross-origin response.

sections.heading: Streaming
sections.text: For long responses, servers can send Transfer-Encoding: chunked or Server-Sent Events (text/event-stream), letting the client render progress incrementally instead of waiting for the whole body. Ryzek's /api/chat/stream uses newline-delimited JSON for live research steps.

topics.example: A 200 with Content-Type: application/json is the normal success response for an API.

topics.title: JSON
topics.summary: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format for structured data: objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. It is the default wire format of web APIs.

sections.heading: Rules
sections.text: Keys must be double-quoted strings, trailing commas are forbidden, and there are no comments or functions. Numbers have no distinction between integer and float at the format level. Text is Unicode, usually UTF-8.

sections.heading: In Python
sections.text: json.loads(s) parses a string into dicts/lists, json.dumps(obj) serialises back, and indent=2 produces readable output. Datetimes and custom objects need a converter. Never use eval() on JSON or untrusted input.

topics.example: {'name': 'Ryzek', 'tools': 12, 'online': true} is a JSON object with three keys.
topics.code:
import json
data = json.loads('{"ok": true, "n": 3}')
print(data['n'])  # 3

topics.title: Databases
topics.summary: A database stores structured data so it can be queried, updated and shared reliably. Relational systems use tables and SQL; NoSQL systems trade some guarantees for flexibility or scale.

sections.heading: Relational model
sections.text: Data lives in tables of rows and columns with a schema. Primary keys identify rows, foreign keys link tables, and indexes speed up lookups. SQL expresses selection, joins, aggregation and transactions.

sections.heading: ACID and transactions
sections.text: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (valid state), Isolation (concurrent transactions don't interfere) and Durability (committed data survives a crash) are the guarantees that make databases safe for money and inventory.

sections.heading: Choosing a store
sections.text: SQLite for a single-app local file, PostgreSQL for general relational work, Redis for caching, Elasticsearch or a vector store for search, and document stores for flexible schemas. Index design and query plans matter more than the brand.

topics.example: SELECT title FROM articles WHERE topic = 'AI' ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 10;

topics.title: Git version control
topics.summary: Git is a distributed version-control system that records snapshots (commits) of your files, so you can branch, merge, compare and roll back.

sections.heading: Core model
sections.text: A commit is a snapshot plus a pointer to its parents, identified by a hash. A branch is just a movable pointer to a commit. The staging area lets you choose exactly which changes go into the next commit.

sections.heading: Everyday workflow
sections.text: git status to inspect, git add to stage, git commit -m to record, git pull to integrate, git push to publish. Create a branch for each feature, open a pull request for review, and merge after tests pass.

sections.heading: Safety habits
sections.text: Commit small and often, write useful messages, never commit secrets (use .env and .gitignore), and use git log / git diff / git restore to investigate and recover. Rebase rewrites history, so avoid it on shared branches.

topics.example: git add . && git commit -m 'Add Ryzek AI research pipeline'

topics.title: Algorithms and complexity
topics.summary: An algorithm is a finite, unambiguous sequence of steps transforming input into output. Complexity describes how its runtime or memory grows with input size.

sections.heading: Big O
sections.text: O(1) constant, O(log n) logarithmic (binary search), O(n) linear, O(n log n) efficient sorting, O(n^2) nested loops, O(2^n) brute-force subsets. Big O ignores constants and describes the dominant term for large n.

sections.heading: Classic strategies
sections.text: Divide and conquer (merge sort), greedy (choose the locally best step), dynamic programming (cache overlapping subproblems), two pointers, sliding window, and graph traversal (BFS for shortest unweighted paths, DFS for exploration).

sections.heading: Correctness
sections.text: Prove a loop invariant, handle empty and boundary inputs, test against a brute-force reference on small cases, and measure with realistic data rather than guessing from Big O alone.

topics.example: Binary search finds an item in a sorted million-element array in about 20 comparisons, not 500,000.

topics.title: Data structures
topics.summary: A data structure organises data so particular operations are fast. Choosing the right one is often the difference between O(n) and O(1).

sections.heading: The essentials
sections.text: Arrays/lists give O(1) indexed access but O(n) insertion in the middle. Hash maps (Python dicts) give average O(1) lookup/insert. Stacks are LIFO, queues FIFO. Linked lists give O(1) insertion with a pointer but poor locality.

sections.heading: Trees and graphs
sections.text: Binary search trees keep keys ordered; balanced variants (AVL, red-black) guarantee O(log n). Heaps give O(1) min/max and O(log n) insert. Graphs model relationships with vertices and edges, stored as adjacency lists or matrices.

sections.heading: In Python
sections.text: list, dict, set, tuple, collections.deque for queues, heapq for priority queues, and dataclasses for records. A set gives O(1) membership tests and deduplication.

topics.example: Use a set to check 'have I seen this user?' instead of scanning a list every time.

topics.title: Cryptography and encryption
topics.summary: Cryptography protects information using mathematical transformations and keys. Encryption provides confidentiality; hashing provides integrity; signatures provide authenticity.

sections.heading: Symmetric vs asymmetric
sections.text: Symmetric ciphers (AES) use one shared secret and are fast for bulk data. Asymmetric cryptography (RSA, elliptic curves) uses a public/private key pair and is slower, so it is used to exchange keys and sign data, not to encrypt large files.

sections.heading: Hashing
sections.text: A hash function maps data to a fixed-length digest. Cryptographic hashes are one-way and collision-resistant. Passwords must be stored with slow salted hashes (bcrypt, Argon2), never with fast hashes like SHA-256 alone.

sections.heading: TLS in practice
sections.text: HTTPS uses TLS: the server proves identity with a certificate, the client and server negotiate a symmetric session key, and all HTTP traffic is encrypted. The padlock means the connection is protected, not that the site is trustworthy.

topics.example: Never put an API key in source code; keep it in an environment variable and rotate it if exposed.

topics.title: Operating systems
topics.summary: An operating system manages hardware and provides abstractions - processes, files, memory and sockets - so applications can run without knowing the details of the machine.

sections.heading: Core responsibilities
sections.text: Process scheduling and isolation, virtual memory, file systems, device drivers, networking and permissions. The kernel runs in privileged mode; user programs make system calls to request services.

sections.heading: Processes and threads
sections.text: A process has its own address space; threads share it. Context switching, locks, semaphores and message passing coordinate concurrency. Race conditions and deadlocks are the classic bugs.

sections.heading: Virtual memory
sections.text: Each process sees a private address space mapped to physical RAM and disk by the MMU. Paging enables isolation, swapping and copy-on-write. Cache locality often dominates real performance.

topics.example: When Ryzek handles two chats at once, a threaded HTTP server gives each request its own thread in the same process.

topics.title: Computer networks and the internet
topics.summary: The internet is a global network of networks that moves data in packets. IP addresses routes them, TCP makes delivery reliable, and DNS maps names to addresses.

sections.heading: Layered model
sections.text: Application (HTTP, DNS), transport (TCP, UDP, QUIC), internet (IP), and link (Ethernet, Wi-Fi). Each layer adds a header and hands the packet down; the receiver strips headers going up. Encapsulation keeps concerns separate.

sections.heading: TCP and DNS
sections.text: TCP establishes a connection with a three-way handshake, numbers bytes, retransmits losses and controls congestion. UDP is faster but unreliable, used for video and DNS lookups. DNS is a distributed hierarchy of name servers with caching.

sections.heading: Practical debugging
sections.text: ping checks reachability, traceroute shows the path, curl shows HTTP exchanges, and nslookup/dig inspect DNS. Most 'the site is down' problems are DNS, TLS certificates or a firewall, not the application.

topics.example: Typing a domain triggers a DNS lookup, a TCP/TLS handshake, then an HTTP GET.

topics.title: Photosynthesis
topics.summary: Photosynthesis is the process by which plants, algae and cyanobacteria convert light energy into chemical energy stored in carbohydrates, releasing oxygen as a by-product.

sections.heading: Two stages
sections.text: In the light-dependent reactions, chlorophyll in thylakoid membranes absorbs photons, splits water and produces ATP and NADPH while releasing O2. In the Calvin cycle, the enzyme RuBisCO fixes CO2 into organic molecules using that ATP and NADPH to build sugars.

sections.heading: The overall equation
sections.text: 6 CO2 + 6 H2O + light energy -> C6H12O6 + 6 O2. Pigments absorb mostly red and blue wavelengths and reflect green, which is why leaves look green.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: It is the base of most food chains and the main source of atmospheric oxygen. C4 and CAM plants evolved additional carbon-concentrating mechanisms to reduce photorespiration in hot, dry conditions.

topics.example: A leaf in sunlight is a solar-powered chemical factory: water in, sugar and oxygen out.

topics.title: Black holes
topics.summary: A black hole is a region of spacetime where gravity is so intense that nothing, not even light, can escape once it crosses the event horizon.

sections.heading: How they form
sections.text: Stellar-mass black holes form when a massive star exhausts its nuclear fuel and its core collapses under gravity, sometimes triggering a supernova. Supermassive black holes of millions to billions of solar masses sit at the centres of most large galaxies, including Sagittarius A* in the Milky Way.

sections.heading: Key ideas
sections.text: The event horizon is the boundary of no return, at the Schwarzschild radius for a non-rotating hole. General relativity predicts a singularity where curvature diverges. Time dilation becomes extreme near the horizon. Hawking radiation predicts extremely slow evaporation.

sections.heading: How we detect them
sections.text: By observing accretion disks X-ray emissions, stellar orbits around an invisible mass, gravitational lensing, and gravitational waves from mergers detected by LIGO and Virgo. The first direct image of a black hole's shadow was released by the Event Horizon Telescope in 2019.

topics.example: If the Sun became a black hole of the same mass, Earth's orbit would not change - only the light and heat would disappear.

topics.title: Gravity
topics.summary: Gravity is the attraction between masses. Newton modelled it as a force; Einstein explained it as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy.

sections.heading: Newton's law
sections.text: F = G m1 m2 / r^2: force grows with the product of masses and falls with the square of distance. It explains falling objects, tides, planetary orbits and the inverse-square structure of the solar system.

sections.heading: General relativity
sections.text: Mass-energy curves spacetime, and objects follow geodesics in that geometry. It predicts the bending of light, gravitational time dilation, black holes and gravitational waves - all confirmed experimentally. GPS satellites must correct for relativistic time drift.

sections.heading: Open questions
sections.text: Gravity is not yet reconciled with quantum mechanics. Dark matter is inferred from gravitational effects on galaxies, and dark energy from the accelerating expansion of the universe.

topics.example: Near Earth's surface gravity gives about 9.81 m/s^2, so a dropped object gains roughly 9.8 m/s of speed each second.

topics.title: The human brain
topics.summary: The human brain is an organ of roughly 86 billion neurons and a comparable number of glial cells, consuming about 20% of the body's energy while being only about 2% of its mass.

sections.heading: How neurons work
sections.text: Neurons receive signals on dendrites, integrate them and fire an action potential down the axon when a threshold is reached. Synapses transmit chemically via neurotransmitters. Learning changes synaptic strength, a property called plasticity.

sections.heading: Major structures
sections.text: The cerebrum handles language, reasoning and voluntary movement; the cerebral cortex is folded into lobes. The cerebellum coordinates motion, the brainstem controls vital functions, and the hippocampus is central to forming new memories.

sections.heading: Comparison with AI
sections.text: Artificial neural networks are loosely inspired by neurons but are vastly simpler, trained by gradient descent rather than development and experience, and run on digital hardware with different energy and parallelism characteristics.

topics.example: Practice strengthens frequently used circuits, which is why spaced repetition beats cramming for memory.

topics.title: Electricity and circuits
topics.summary: Electricity is the flow of electric charge, usually electrons in a conductor. Voltage is the energy per unit charge, current is the rate of flow, and resistance opposes it.

sections.heading: Ohm's law
sections.text: V = I R links voltage (volts), current (amperes) and resistance (ohms). Power is P = V I = I^2 R. Series circuits share current and add resistance; parallel circuits share voltage and add conductance.

sections.heading: AC and DC
sections.text: Direct current flows one way (batteries, electronics). Alternating current reverses periodically and is used for the grid because transformers can step voltage up for efficient long-distance transmission and down for safe use.

sections.heading: Safety
sections.text: Current, not voltage alone, is dangerous; wet skin lowers resistance dramatically. Fuses, circuit breakers, grounding and residual-current devices interrupt faults and provide a safe path for stray current.

topics.example: A 9 V battery across a 3 ohm resistor drives 3 A and dissipates 27 W as heat.

topics.title: Climate change and the greenhouse effect
topics.summary: Climate change refers to long-term shifts in temperature and weather patterns. The current warming trend is driven primarily by human greenhouse-gas emissions since the industrial revolution.

sections.heading: Mechanism
sections.text: Sunlight warms the surface, which radiates infrared energy back out. Greenhouse gases (CO2, methane, water vapour, nitrous oxide) absorb and re-emit some of that infrared, trapping heat. More CO2 strengthens the effect; the energy imbalance warms the ocean, land and atmosphere.

sections.heading: Evidence
sections.text: Instrumental temperature records, melting glaciers and ice sheets, rising sea level from thermal expansion and land ice loss, ocean heat content, earlier springs, and the isotopic signature of fossil-fuel CO2 all point to the same cause.

sections.heading: Responses
sections.text: Mitigation cuts emissions via energy transition, efficiency, electrification and land use. Adaptation prepares for impacts already locked in. Climate models project ranges of warming depending on future emissions pathways.

topics.example: CO2 concentration rose from about 280 ppm before industrialisation to over 420 ppm today.

topics.title: Water
topics.summary: Water is H2O: two hydrogen atoms covalently bonded to one oxygen. Its polar molecule and hydrogen bonding give it unusual properties that make life possible.

sections.heading: Why it is unusual
sections.text: Hydrogen bonds produce a high specific heat capacity, high surface tension, strong cohesion and adhesion, and an excellent ability to dissolve ionic and polar substances. Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats and insulates lakes.

sections.heading: Key numbers
sections.text: It boils at 100 C and freezes at 0 C at one atmosphere, is densest near 4 C, and has a pH of 7 when pure. The water cycle - evaporation, condensation, precipitation and collection - moves it through the environment.

sections.heading: For humans
sections.text: The adult body is roughly 60% water; it regulates temperature, transports nutrients and removes waste. Access to safe drinking water and sanitation is a major global public-health issue.

topics.example: Sweating cools you because evaporating water carries away a large amount of heat.

topics.title: Islam
topics.summary: Islam is a monotheistic religion centred on submission to God, called Allah in Arabic. Its followers are known as Muslims. According to Islamic tradition, the Prophet Muhammad received the revelations collected in the Quran, which Muslims regard as the word of God. Islam is the second-largest religion in the world and includes many cultures, languages and schools of thought.

sections.heading: Core beliefs
sections.text: Muslims affirm the oneness of God and the prophethood of Muhammad. Islamic teaching also honours earlier prophets, including Adam, Abraham, Moses and Jesus, and regards the Quran as the final revelation in a long line of scriptures. Belief in angels, revealed books, prophets, the Day of Judgement and divine decree are commonly listed as articles of faith. These are statements about what Muslims believe, not claims about which tradition is correct.

sections.heading: The five pillars
sections.text: The five pillars are widely taught as the framework of Muslim practice. They are the declaration of faith, the five daily prayers, almsgiving, fasting during the month of Ramadan, and the pilgrimage to Mecca for those who are able. Practice varies across communities and individuals, and details of ritual and jurisprudence are worked out in different schools of Islamic law.

sections.heading: Texts and sources
sections.text: The Quran is the central scripture of Islam, written in Arabic and arranged in 114 chapters called surahs. The hadith are reports about the words and actions of the Prophet Muhammad and are used alongside the Quran in Islamic scholarship. Muslims differ over the authority and interpretation of particular reports, so careful writing attributes a view to its school or source rather than presenting it as universal.

sections.heading: History and spread
sections.text: Islam arose in the Arabian Peninsula in the seventh century. The migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar. Over following centuries, Muslim societies spread across West Asia, North Africa, Central Asia, South Asia and beyond, producing influential work in mathematics, medicine, architecture, law, philosophy and literature.

sections.heading: Diversity within the tradition
sections.text: Islam contains many communities and interpretations. Sunni and Shia are the two largest broad traditions, and each contains further schools of law, theology and spirituality, including Sufi orders. Differences concern questions of leadership, authority and legal method. A neutral account describes these differences without ranking them or declaring any group right or wrong.

sections.heading: Respectful language
sections.text: When writing about Islam, use courteous terms, capitalise the names of scriptures and prophets, and avoid jokes, caricatures or dismissive generalisations. Many Muslims add an honorific such as 'peace be upon him' after the name of a prophet. An AI assistant can reproduce such honorifics when asked, but it should not issue religious rulings; those belong to qualified scholars.

topics.title: Prophet Muhammad
topics.summary: In Islamic tradition, Muhammad is the final prophet and messenger of God, born in Mecca around 570 CE and who died in Medina in 632 CE. Muslims believe the Quran was revealed to him over roughly twenty-three years. He is held in the highest reverence by Muslims, who commonly add an honorific such as 'peace be upon him' after his name.

sections.heading: Life according to Islamic sources
sections.text: Biographical accounts describe Muhammad as born into the Quraysh tribe of Mecca around 570 CE, orphaned at a young age, and known for trustworthiness in his work as a merchant. Islamic tradition holds that at about the age of forty he began receiving revelations through the angel Gabriel. These reports come from Islamic sources and are described here as matters of faith and tradition, not as independently verified history.

sections.heading: The Meccan and Medinan periods
sections.text: The first phase of preaching in Mecca met strong opposition, and in 622 CE the community migrated to Medina, an event known as the Hijra that begins the Islamic calendar. In Medina, Muhammad became a religious and political leader, and the community grew. He died in 632 CE. Standard biographies divide his life into these two periods because the character of the revelations and the community's circumstances differed between them.

sections.heading: Teachings and character
sections.text: Islamic sources emphasise monotheism, moral conduct, care for the poor, honesty in trade, the rights of neighbours and the equality of believers before God. Muslims look to his reported sayings and actions, known as hadith and sunnah, as a model for conduct. Accounts of his character are devotional as well as historical, so a neutral summary attributes them to Islamic tradition.

sections.heading: How other traditions view him
sections.text: Muslims regard Muhammad as the final prophet in a line that includes Abraham, Moses and Jesus. Other religious communities have held a range of views about him across history, from theological disagreement to scholarly interest. A respectful account states these as historical positions held by particular communities rather than as verdicts.

sections.heading: Why honour matters
sections.text: For Muslims, the name of a prophet is never used casually or mockingly. Depictions are treated with great care, and verbal or visual mockery is experienced as deeply offensive. Practical guidance: use the full name, add the honorific the reader prefers, avoid images, and never use a prophet's name in a joke, a random example or a dismissive comparison.

sections.heading: Limits of an AI answer
sections.text: An assistant can summarise widely reported biographical facts and describe what Muslims believe, but it is not a religious authority. Questions of law, doctrine, rulings or personal religious practice should be referred to qualified scholars and to a person's own scripture and community. Where historical details are disputed or uncertain, a careful answer says so.

topics.title: The Quran
topics.summary: The Quran is the central scripture of Islam. Muslims believe it is the word of God revealed to the Prophet Muhammad in Arabic over about twenty-three years. It is arranged in 114 chapters called surahs and is recited in prayer, study and devotion by Muslims around the world.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.text: The text is divided into 114 surahs of unequal length, which are further divided into verses called ayat. Except for the opening chapter, the surahs are roughly ordered from longest to shortest rather than chronologically. Recitation follows rules of pronunciation known as tajwid, and memorisation of the whole text is a respected achievement.

sections.heading: Themes
sections.text: Recurring themes include the oneness of God, moral responsibility, mercy, justice, the lives of earlier prophets, the natural world as a sign, and accountability in the afterlife. Stories about figures such as Abraham, Moses, Joseph and Mary also appear. Interpretive traditions differ over the meaning of particular passages.

sections.heading: Reverence and handling
sections.text: Muslims treat the Quran with great care: it is recited with respect, and many perform ablution before handling a written copy. Translations are generally regarded as interpretations of meaning rather than the scripture itself, which is why the Arabic text retains a special status. Mockery, mishandling or disrespectful quotation is deeply offensive to believers.

topics.title: Christianity
topics.summary: Christianity is a monotheistic religion centred on the life and teachings of Jesus of Nazareth, whom Christians call the Christ or Son of God. Its scripture is the Bible, made up of the Old Testament and the New Testament. It is the world's largest religion and includes many traditions, including Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant communities.

sections.heading: Core beliefs
sections.text: Christians believe in one God and, in most traditions, in the Trinity: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Central beliefs concern the incarnation, the crucifixion and the resurrection of Jesus, and salvation through him. These are statements of Christian belief, presented descriptively rather than as a verdict on any tradition.

sections.heading: Scripture
sections.text: The Bible is a library of texts written over many centuries in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek. The New Testament contains the Gospels, Acts, letters and Revelation. Different communities include different books in their Old Testament canons and differ in how they interpret particular passages.

sections.heading: Diversity and history
sections.text: Christianity began in the first century in the eastern Mediterranean and spread across the Roman Empire and beyond. Major divisions developed over centuries, including the split between Eastern Orthodoxy and Roman Catholicism and the later Reformation. A neutral account names these traditions without ranking them or taking sides in their doctrinal disagreements.

sections.heading: Respectful language
sections.text: Use courteous terms for Jesus, the Bible, the Church and believers; avoid jokes or caricatures; and attribute doctrines to the communities that hold them. An AI assistant can describe what Christians believe but should not pronounce on doctrine or give personal spiritual direction.

topics.title: Judaism
topics.summary: Judaism is the religion and cultural tradition of the Jewish people, centred on the covenant between God and Israel and on the teachings of the Torah. It is one of the oldest monotheistic traditions and includes diverse communities with distinct customs, liturgies and interpretations.

sections.heading: Texts and practice
sections.text: The Hebrew Bible, especially the Torah, is foundational, and the Talmud records rabbinic discussion of law and interpretation. Practice includes Sabbath observance, dietary laws, prayer, festivals such as Passover and Yom Kippur, and life-cycle rituals. Observance varies widely across communities.

sections.heading: Community and diversity
sections.text: Jewish communities include Ashkenazi, Sephardi, Mizrahi and many other traditions, as well as a range of religious movements from Orthodox to Reform. A careful account describes these differences without declaring one to be authoritative.

sections.heading: Respectful language
sections.text: Use courteous terms for the Torah, synagogues, rabbis and Jewish people; avoid stereotypes, collective blame and jokes about sacred texts or observance. Antisemitism in any form is unacceptable. An assistant should describe beliefs neutrally and defer questions of law and practice to qualified rabbis and communities.

topics.title: Hinduism
topics.summary: Hinduism is a family of related religious and philosophical traditions originating in the Indian subcontinent. It includes a wide range of beliefs, deities, texts and practices, with concepts such as dharma, karma and moksha playing central roles in many schools.

sections.heading: Texts and ideas
sections.text: The Vedas, Upanishads, epics and Puranas are among the texts regarded as authoritative in different traditions, and the Bhagavad Gita is widely studied. Ideas about dharma, karma, rebirth and liberation are interpreted differently across philosophical schools.

sections.heading: Practice and diversity
sections.text: Practice may include temple worship, household rituals, meditation, pilgrimage, festivals such as Diwali and Holi, and devotion to particular deities. There is no single central authority, so descriptions should name the specific tradition being discussed.

sections.heading: Respectful language
sections.text: Use accurate names for deities, texts and festivals; avoid treating a diverse family of traditions as one uniform belief; and never use sacred names or symbols in jokes or dismissive comparisons.

topics.title: Buddhism
topics.summary: Buddhism is a tradition based on the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama, known as the Buddha, who lived in ancient India. It addresses the nature of suffering and the path to liberation, and it includes Theravada, Mahayana and Vajrayana traditions among others.

sections.heading: Core teachings
sections.text: The Four Noble Truths and the Noble Eightfold Path are widely taught as a framework, alongside concepts such as karma, rebirth, impermanence and dependent origination. Interpretations differ between schools.

sections.heading: Practice
sections.text: Practice commonly includes ethical conduct, meditation, mindfulness, study, monastic discipline and devotion. Communities differ in language, ritual and institutional structure across South, East and Southeast Asia and beyond.

sections.heading: Respectful language
sections.text: Refer to the Buddha and to Buddhist texts and teachers courteously; avoid using images or names of the Buddha as decoration or humour; and describe schools by their own names rather than ranking them.

topics.title: Sikhism
topics.summary: Sikhism is a monotheistic religion founded in the Punjab region of South Asia in the fifteenth century, associated with Guru Nanak and the ten Sikh Gurus. The Guru Granth Sahib is regarded as the eternal Guru and central scripture.

sections.heading: Teachings
sections.text: Sikh teaching emphasises the oneness of God, remembrance of the divine name, honest work, service to others and equality of all people. The institution of langar, a free community kitchen, expresses these commitments in practice.

sections.heading: Scripture and community
sections.text: The Guru Granth Sahib contains hymns by the Sikh Gurus and by saints from diverse backgrounds. It is treated with the highest reverence in a gurdwara. The Khalsa and the five articles of faith are important to initiated Sikhs.

sections.heading: Respectful language
sections.text: Use correct names for the Gurus, the scripture and the gurdwara; avoid jokes about articles of faith or Sikh names; and describe Sikh beliefs using Sikh sources and terms.

topics.title: Respectful discussion of religions and prophets
topics.summary: Respectful discussion of religions means describing beliefs accurately, attributing claims to the communities that hold them, and avoiding mockery, caricature, ranking or sectarian judgement. It applies to every faith, every prophet, every scripture and every believer.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Religious commitments are deeply personal and often tied to identity, family and community. Careless wording can cause real hurt even when no harm was intended. Accuracy and courtesy are not opposed: a neutral description of what a community believes is both more respectful and more factually reliable than a verdict on whether it is right.

sections.heading: Practical rules for writing
sections.text: Use the names and terms a community uses for itself; capitalise the names of scriptures, prophets and festivals; attribute beliefs with phrases such as 'in Islamic tradition', 'Christians believe' or 'according to the Hebrew Bible'; and describe internal differences without declaring a winner. Avoid jokes, sarcasm, caricature, collective blame and sweeping generalisations about billions of people.

sections.heading: About prophets specifically
sections.text: Prophets are treated with the highest reverence by their followers. Many Muslims say or write 'peace be upon him', or use the Arabic symbol ﷺ, after the name of a prophet. Never place a prophet's name in a joke, a random example, a dismissive comparison or an image. If a user's question is phrased disrespectfully, answer calmly and do not repeat the insult.

sections.heading: Neutrality and disagreement
sections.text: Where traditions disagree, present each position as a position held by a particular community and dated to a particular context. Do not rank religions, declare any community correct or incorrect, or settle sectarian disputes. An AI assistant is not a scholar, mufti, priest, rabbi or religious authority, and should say so when asked for a ruling.

sections.heading: Handling uncertainty
sections.text: Religious history often involves sources written centuries after events, translations with disputed readings, and traditions that differ over details. A careful answer marks what is well attested, what is a matter of faith, and what is uncertain. It does not invent dates, sayings, rulings or biographical details to fill a gap.

sections.heading: What to do instead of a ruling
sections.text: For questions of religious law, doctrine or personal practice, explain the limits of an assistant, suggest the kinds of primary sources a qualified scholar would use, and refer the person to scholars and to their own scripture and community. This is a practical, useful answer rather than a refusal.
