topics.title: Time travel
topics.summary: Time travel means moving between different points in time in a way that differs from the ordinary one-second-per-second forward progression. Forward time travel is physically real and experimentally confirmed through relativistic time dilation; backward time travel is speculative, faces severe theoretical and observational obstacles, and has no experimental evidence.

sections.heading: Forward time travel is real
sections.text: Special relativity shows that a clock moving at high speed relative to an observer ticks more slowly, and general relativity shows that clocks deeper in a gravitational field also run more slowly. Astronauts and atomic clocks on aircraft measurably age by slightly different amounts. A traveller who moves very fast or stays near a strong gravitational field can therefore arrive in the future while experiencing less personal time.

sections.heading: Backward time travel and closed timelike curves
sections.text: General relativity admits mathematical solutions containing closed timelike curves, which are paths through spacetime that return to their own past. The Godel universe, the Tipler cylinder and traversable wormholes are examples. Each requires physical conditions that appear unrealistic, such as infinite cylinders, exotic matter with negative energy density, or a rotating universe.

sections.heading: Paradoxes
sections.text: The grandfather paradox asks what happens if a traveller prevents their own existence, and the bootstrap paradox asks where information in a self-causing loop originally came from. Proposed resolutions include the Novikov self-consistency principle, which permits only consistent histories, and many-worlds style branching, in which changes create a different history. Neither has been experimentally tested.

sections.heading: Why most physicists are sceptical
sections.text: Stephen Hawking proposed the chronology protection conjecture, suggesting that the laws of physics prevent closed timelike curves from forming on macroscopic scales. Quantum effects near a would-be time machine may diverge and destroy it. No signal, object or traveller from the future has ever been reliably observed.

sections.heading: Common misconceptions
sections.text: Relativity does not permit faster-than-light travel simply by going very fast, because energy requirements diverge as speed approaches light speed. Seeing distant stars is looking into the past in the sense of receiving old light, but it is not travelling to that past. Cryonics and suspended animation are not time travel in the relativistic sense.

sections.heading: In culture and in research
sections.text: H. G. Wells's short novel The Time Machine established much of the modern vocabulary of the idea. Later fiction explores branching timelines, fixed loops and alternate histories. Serious research continues on the arrow of time, quantum gravity, causality and the thermodynamics of information rather than on building a machine.

topics.title: English poetry
topics.summary: English poetry is the body of verse written in the English language from the Old English period to the present. It includes epic and elegy, sonnet and ballad, metrical verse and free verse, and movements ranging from the Renaissance and Romanticism to Modernism, the Beat generation and contemporary spoken word.

sections.heading: Major periods
sections.text: Old English verse such as Beowulf used alliterative stress rather than rhyme. The Renaissance brought blank verse and the sonnet, with Geoffrey Chaucer, William Shakespeare and John Milton as central figures. The Romantic period reacted against industrial rationality, the Victorian age favoured narrative and dramatic monologue, and Modernism broke regular metre after the First World War.

sections.heading: Major poets
sections.text: Frequently studied poets include Chaucer, Shakespeare, Milton, John Donne, William Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, John Keats, Percy Bysshe Shelley, Lord Byron, Alfred Tennyson, Robert Browning, Emily Dickinson, Walt Whitman, W. B. Yeats, T. S. Eliot, Ezra Pound, Robert Frost, W. H. Auden, Langston Hughes, Sylvia Plath, Maya Angelou and Seamus Heaney.

sections.heading: Forms
sections.text: Common forms include the sonnet, the ballad, the ode, the elegy, the epic, the villanelle, the limerick, blank verse, heroic couplets and free verse. Each form carries conventions about line count, rhyme scheme, metre and argument, and poets often gain meaning by obeying or deliberately breaking those conventions.

sections.heading: Technique
sections.text: English verse relies on stress-based metre, especially iambic pentameter, alongside rhyme, assonance, alliteration, caesura, enjambment, imagery, metaphor and symbol. A line break can create emphasis or ambiguity without adding a word, which is the main reason poetry differs from prose.

sections.heading: How to read a poem
sections.text: Read it aloud once for sound, identify the speaker and the situation, paraphrase the literal argument, then track where the imagery or the metre shifts. That shift usually marks the turn, the moment where the poem's real claim appears.

topics.title: Poetic forms and metres
topics.summary: A poetic form is a recognisable set of conventions governing line length, stanza structure, rhyme and metre. English poetry inherited classical and European forms and later developed free verse, while Urdu poetry developed its own family of forms built on the ghazal, the nazm and the classical aruz system of quantitative metre.

sections.heading: English stanza forms
sections.text: The sonnet has fourteen lines; the Shakespearean form uses three quatrains and a closing couplet, while the Petrarchan form uses an octave and a sestet. The ballad traditionally uses alternating four- and three-stress lines, the villanelle repeats two refrain lines across nineteen lines, and the limerick is a five-line comic form with a tight rhyme pattern.

sections.heading: English metres
sections.text: Iambic pentameter contains five iambs, each an unstressed syllable followed by a stressed one. Blank verse is unrhymed iambic pentameter, and the heroic couplet is a pair of rhymed pentameter lines. Trochaic, anapaestic and dactylic metres create very different rhythms, and accentual verse counts stresses rather than syllables.

sections.heading: Urdu forms
sections.text: The ghazal is a sequence of autonomous couplets sharing a refrain and rhyme. The nazm is a continuous poem with a single theme, the qasida is a panegyric or formal ode, the masnavi is a long narrative in rhyming couplets, the marsia is an elegy, the rubai is a four-line quatrain, and the doha and the sher are short standalone units.

sections.heading: Urdu prosody
sections.text: Classical Urdu verse uses aruz, a quantitative system measuring long and short syllables rather than stress. A ghazal fixes the qafia, the rhyming word before the refrain, and the radif, the repeated refrain itself. Matching the metre while keeping both is the central technical challenge of writing a ghazal.

sections.heading: Free verse and prose poetry
sections.text: Free verse abandons regular metre and rhyme but keeps deliberate lineation and rhythm. Prose poetry uses paragraphs rather than lines while keeping poetic density, image and compression. Both became dominant in the twentieth century and remain common in contemporary work.

topics.title: The sonnet
topics.summary: A sonnet is a fourteen-line poem, traditionally in iambic pentameter, that presents an argument or an emotional situation and resolves or complicates it at a turn called the volta. It originated in thirteenth-century Italy, was perfected by Petrarch, and was adapted into English by Wyatt, Surrey and Shakespeare.

sections.heading: Structure
sections.text: The Petrarchan sonnet divides into an octave rhyming abbaabba and a sestet with a flexible pattern, and the volta usually arrives between them. The Shakespearean sonnet uses abab cdcd efef gg, so three quatrains develop an idea and a final couplet delivers a summary, a twist or a judgement.

sections.heading: The volta
sections.text: The turn is the poem's hinge: a question becomes an answer, a complaint becomes a resolution, or a claim is quietly reversed. Reading a sonnet well means locating the volta and explaining what changes across it.

sections.heading: Notable sequences
sections.text: Shakespeare's 154 sonnets, Sidney's Astrophil and Stella, Spenser's Amoretti, Milton's occasional sonnets, Wordsworth's political sonnets, Elizabeth Barrett Browning's Sonnets from the Portuguese and Edna St Vincent Millay's sonnets show the form's range across four centuries.

sections.heading: Modern use
sections.text: Modern poets keep the fourteen-line frame while loosening metre and rhyme, using the form for irony, portraiture and political argument. The compression of space is the point: a strict container makes a small shift feel large.

topics.title: Haiku and short verse forms
topics.summary: Short verse forms achieve concentration by strict economy. The Japanese haiku, the tanka, the English limerick, the epigram and the Urdu rubai each use very few lines but carry conventions that give those lines disproportionate weight.

sections.heading: Haiku
sections.text: A traditional Japanese haiku has seventeen sound units arranged in a five-seven-five pattern, a seasonal word known as kigo, and a cutting word or juxtaposition known as kireji. Matsuo Basho, Yosa Buson and Kobayashi Issa are the classic masters. English haiku often relax the syllable count and keep the seasonal image and the juxtaposition instead.

sections.heading: Tanka and related forms
sections.text: Tanka adds two longer lines to the haiku pattern for a total of thirty-one sound units and often turns on a personal response. Renga and haikai are collaborative linked-verse chains built from alternating stanzas. Senryu resembles haiku but addresses human foibles rather than nature.

sections.heading: Limerick and epigram
sections.text: The limerick is a five-line comic verse with an aabba rhyme and a strongly anapestic rhythm, popularised by Edward Lear. The epigram is a very short, pointed poem or statement that ends in wit or reversal, practised by Martial, John Donne, Alexander Pope and later by Stevie Smith and Dorothy Parker.

sections.heading: Rubai and doha
sections.text: The rubai is a four-line Urdu or Persian quatrain in which the first, second and fourth lines usually rhyme, and it often carries a philosophical or mystical point. The doha is a couplet in Hindi and Urdu used for concise moral or devotional statement, famously by Kabir and Rahim.

topics.title: Romantic poetry
topics.summary: Romanticism was a literary movement roughly spanning the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries that privileged imagination, emotion, nature, individual consciousness and the ordinary language of common life against industrial rationalism and neoclassical rules.

sections.heading: Core ideas
sections.text: Wordsworth defined poetry as the spontaneous overflow of powerful feelings recollected in tranquillity and argued for the language of ordinary people. Coleridge explored the supernatural and the imagination. Keats pursued sensuous beauty and negative capability, the ability to remain in uncertainty without reaching for fixed answers.

sections.heading: Major figures
sections.text: The first generation includes William Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge and William Blake. The second includes John Keats, Percy Bysshe Shelley and Lord Byron. Their work ranges from lyrical ballads and odes to long philosophical dramas and satirical narrative.

sections.heading: Forms and technique
sections.text: Romantics revived the sonnet, the ode and the ballad, and used blank verse for meditative long poems. Vivid natural imagery, symbolic landscapes, apostrophe and a speaking self replaced the public, declarative voice of eighteenth-century verse.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.text: Romantic ideas about authenticity, childhood, the sublime and the artist's social role shaped Victorian, American Transcendentalist and modern poetry. The movement also established the modern expectation that a poem expresses an individual consciousness.

topics.title: Modernist and free verse poetry
topics.summary: Modernist poetry broke with regular metre, linear narrative and the unified lyrical self in the early twentieth century. Imagism, fragmentation, allusion, collage and free verse replaced ornament, and the poem became a constructed object rather than a continuous confession.

sections.heading: Imagism
sections.text: Ezra Pound, H. D. and Amy Lowell called for direct treatment of the thing, no word that did not contribute, and musical phrasing rather than a metronome. The image, not the argument, became the unit of composition.

sections.heading: Major works and poets
sections.text: T. S. Eliot's The Waste Land used collage and multiple voices to register cultural dislocation, while W. B. Yeats combined symbol, myth and political history. Wallace Stevens, William Carlos Williams, Marianne Moore, e. e. cummings, Langston Hughes and later the Beat poets pushed the idiom further.

sections.heading: Free verse
sections.text: Free verse has no fixed metre or rhyme but keeps deliberate line breaks, cadence and pattern. Its difficulty is discipline: without a given form the poet must build rhythm and structure from repetition, syntax and spacing.

sections.heading: After Modernism
sections.text: Confessional poets such as Sylvia Plath and Robert Lowell turned to personal history; the Beats favoured open form and performance; the Black Arts movement linked poetry to political community; and contemporary spoken word and slam poetry returned the poem to the stage.

topics.title: American poetry
topics.summary: American poetry developed its own voice in the nineteenth century and became a major force in world literature, characterised by experimentation with line, an interest in democracy and identity, and a strong tradition of public performance.

sections.heading: Nineteenth century
sections.text: Walt Whitman's Leaves of Grass used long free-verse lines and an expansive speaking self, while Emily Dickinson used compact hymn-like stanzas, slant rhyme and radical compression. Their opposite approaches defined two durable possibilities for American verse.

sections.heading: Twentieth century
sections.text: Robert Frost used traditional metre with New England speech, Ezra Pound and T. S. Eliot led Modernist experimentation, Langston Hughes fused jazz and blues rhythms with the Harlem Renaissance, and Wallace Stevens made imagination itself the subject.

sections.heading: Later voices
sections.text: Gwendolyn Brooks, Allen Ginsberg, Sylvia Plath, Maya Angelou, Adrienne Rich, Billy Collins, Rita Dove, Joy Harjo and many others broadened the canon across region, race, gender, language and form.

sections.heading: Performance and the present
sections.text: Spoken word, poetry slams and hip hop lyrics emphasise breath, rhythm and audience. Many contemporary poets move between page and stage, and between English and other languages within a single poem.

topics.title: Urdu poetry
topics.summary: Urdu poetry is one of the richest vernacular poetic traditions in the world, developed from the eighteenth century onward in Delhi, Lucknow, Deccan and later across South Asia. It is built chiefly on the ghazal and the nazm, uses the quantitative aruz metres, and is performed publicly at a mushaira.

sections.heading: Historical development
sections.text: Wali Deccani carried the southern Rekhta tradition north to Delhi, where Mir Taqi Mir, Sauda and Dard established the classical idiom. The Delhi school gave way to the Lucknow school, associated with elegance and diction, and Mirza Ghalib united both with philosophical depth. The nineteenth and twentieth centuries added political, nationalist and progressive voices.

sections.heading: Forms
sections.text: The ghazal links autonomous couplets through a shared rhyme and refrain; the nazm sustains one theme across a continuous structure; the qasida praises or argues formally; the masnavi narrates at length; the marsia mourns; the rubai compresses a thought into four lines; and the doha and the sher offer standalone compression.

sections.heading: Prosody and craft
sections.text: Aruz measures long and short syllables in fixed patterns called bahar. A ghazal sets a qafia, the rhyming word, and a radif, the repeated refrain. The poet must keep metre, qafia and radif in every couplet while making each sher independently meaningful. A matla is the opening couplet that establishes the pattern, and a maqta is the closing couplet that often carries the poet's pen name, or takhallus.

sections.heading: Major poets
sections.text: Mir Taqi Mir, Mirza Ghalib, Momin, Dard, Sauda, Daagh Dehlvi, Bahadur Shah Zafar, Allama Iqbal, Josh Malihabadi, Firaq Gorakhpuri, Jigar Moradabadi, Hasrat Mohani, Faiz Ahmed Faiz, Sahir Ludhianvi, Kaifi Azmi, Ahmad Nadeem Qasmi, Nida Fazli, Munir Niazi, Ahmad Faraz, Parveen Shakir, Iftikhar Arif and Jaun Elia are among the most widely read names.

sections.heading: Themes
sections.text: Classical imagery centres on the beloved, the wine-bearer, the garden, the nightingale, the desert, separation and union, and the wound of longing. Many poems work simultaneously as romantic, mystical and philosophical statements, which is why the same sher can be read at several levels.

sections.heading: Performance
sections.text: A mushaira is a gathering where poets recite ghazals and nazms and the audience responds between couplets with appreciation or requests for a repeat. Tarannum, a melodic recitation style, and the speed of audience response shape how a poem is written and revised.

sections.heading: Reading and translation
sections.text: Urdu is written in a Perso-Arabic script, and much classical poetry draws on Persian vocabulary. Translation has to negotiate rhyme, refrain, metre and layered meaning at once; a literal translation often loses the radif, so good translations usually add a short note on the form.

topics.title: The ghazal
topics.summary: The ghazal is a poem of autonomous rhyming couplets, usually between five and fifteen, that share a metre, a rhyme and a refrain. Originating in Arabic and perfected in Persian and Urdu, it is the most recognised form of Urdu poetry and has also been adopted by poets writing in English.

sections.heading: Formal rules
sections.text: Every couplet, or sher, is a complete poem in itself. The first couplet, the matla, states the rhyme in both lines; in later couplets only the second line carries it. The qafia is the rhyming word immediately before the radif, and the radif is the repeated word or phrase that closes the line.

sections.heading: Structure and naming
sections.text: The maqta is the final couplet, where the poet often includes a takhallus, a pen name. The bahr is the chosen quantitative metre. A ghazal that omits the radif is called ghair-muraddaf, while one with a refrain is muraddaf.

sections.heading: How meaning works
sections.text: Because each sher stands alone, a ghazal advances by resonance rather than narrative. Traditional imagery of the beloved, the candle, the moth, the desert, the tavern and the garden can be read as romantic, mystical, social or philosophical, often at the same time.

sections.heading: Masters
sections.text: Mir Taqi Mir is celebrated for the plain intensity of grief, Mirza Ghalib for metaphysical wit, Daagh for idiom and elegance, Firaq Gorakhpuri for classical craft, Faiz Ahmed Faiz for joining romantic diction to political hope, and Ahmad Faraz and Parveen Shakir for a modern, direct voice.

sections.heading: The ghazal in English
sections.text: Poets such as Adrienne Rich, Agha Shahid Ali, Robert Bly and John Hollander have written English ghazals, often relaxing the quantitative metre while keeping the autonomous couplets, the refrain and the poet's signature in the closing sher.

topics.title: Nazm and other Urdu verse forms
topics.summary: Beyond the ghazal, Urdu poetry uses several forms with distinct purposes: the nazm for sustained argument, the qasida for formal praise, the masnavi for narrative, the marsia for elegy, and the rubai and doha for compression.

sections.heading: Nazm
sections.text: A nazm is a continuous poem with a single subject and a developing structure, so its lines depend on one another rather than standing alone. It may use any metre and rhyme scheme, including free verse. Allama Iqbal, Faiz Ahmed Faiz, Josh Malihabadi and Nida Fazli used it for philosophical, political and lyrical arguments.

sections.heading: Qasida and masnavi
sections.text: The qasida is a long formal poem, often panegyric, that moves through set thematic sections and maintains one rhyme throughout. The masnavi uses rhyming couplets with a changing rhyme, which makes it suitable for long narrative; classical examples include religious, romantic and historical stories.

sections.heading: Marsia and rubai
sections.text: The marsia is an elegiac poem, historically associated with commemorating the tragedy of Karbala and developed to great length by Mir Anis and Mirza Dabeer. The rubai is a four-line stanza, usually with the first, second and fourth lines rhyming, that delivers a complete thought with epigrammatic force.

sections.heading: Short forms
sections.text: The doha is a self-contained couplet used for moral or devotional statement, and the sher is the two-line unit from which a ghazal is built. A qata is a short fragment of two or four lines that does not form a full ghazal.

sections.heading: Choosing a form
sections.text: Use a ghazal when each couplet should stand alone, a nazm when the argument must accumulate, a masnavi when telling a story, and a rubai when a single idea needs to land sharply. The choice of form is part of the meaning, not just the packaging.

topics.title: Mirza Ghalib
topics.summary: Mirza Asadullah Khan Ghalib, known simply as Ghalib, was a nineteenth-century Urdu and Persian poet generally regarded as the greatest classical master of the Urdu ghazal. He lived through the decline of Mughal Delhi and the upheaval of 1857, and his work combines emotional intensity with philosophical wit.

sections.heading: Life
sections.text: Ghalib was born in Agra in 1797 and spent most of his adult life in Delhi. He outlived the Mughal court's patronage, struggled with pension disputes and debt, and recorded the upheaval of his age in letters and in Persian prose as well as in verse.

sections.heading: Poetic character
sections.text: His ghazals are famous for difficulty, compressed paradox, metaphysical questioning and an ironic self-awareness. He treats love, loss, certainty, doubt, divine unity and the instability of the self with a voice that can be tender and sceptical within the same couplet.

sections.heading: Works
sections.text: His Urdu Diwan is relatively small but extraordinarily influential. His Persian poetry, his collections of letters and his prose accounts of the rebellion are also studied, and his letters are admired for their colloquial, lively Urdu prose.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.text: Later poets from Iqbal and Faiz to Parveen Shakir and Jaun Elia have measured themselves against him. His couplets are quoted across South Asia in everyday conversation, in music, and in both scholarly and popular readings of the ghazal.

topics.title: Allama Iqbal
topics.summary: Allama Iqbal was a poet, philosopher and barrister whose Urdu and Persian verse reshaped South Asian literary and intellectual life in the early twentieth century. He is best known for the concept of khudi, or selfhood, developed as a spiritual and ethical force rather than mere ego.

sections.heading: Life and work
sections.text: Born in Sialkot in 1877, he studied in Lahore and then in Cambridge, Munich and Heidelberg before returning to practise law and write. His collections include Bang-e-Dara, Bal-e-Jibril, Zarb-e-Kalim in Urdu and Asrar-e-Khudi and Javid Nama in Persian.

sections.heading: Khudi
sections.text: Khudi names the cultivated, disciplined self that becomes capable of creative action and nearness to the divine. Iqbal contrasts it with self-negation and with passive imitation, and he presents love, action and restless striving as the forces that strengthen it.

sections.heading: Poetic style
sections.text: He uses the classical ghazal and nazm with a new public, philosophical voice, drawing on Quranic and Persian imagery, European philosophy and the political concerns of his age. Well-known poems include Shikwa, Jawab-e-Shikwa, Tulu-e-Islam and the lyrics of Bal-e-Jibril.

sections.heading: Reception
sections.text: His poetry is read both as literature and as a statement of Muslim intellectual revival, and it is widely quoted, sung and translated. Because his work crosses devotional, philosophical and political registers, a careful summary attributes interpretations to their readers rather than settling them.

topics.title: Mir Taqi Mir and the classical Delhi school
topics.summary: Mir Taqi Mir is often called the pioneer of the Urdu ghazal's emotional idiom. Writing in eighteenth-century Delhi alongside Sauda, Dard and Momin, he established a plain, inward, grief-saturated style that later poets treated as the benchmark of authenticity.

sections.heading: The Delhi school
sections.text: Wali Deccani's visit to Delhi helped establish Rekhta as a literary language there. Mir, Sauda and Dard developed distinct voices: Mir for inward sorrow and simplicity, Sauda for satire and rhetorical scale, and Dard for mystical restraint.

sections.heading: Mir's language
sections.text: His diction is deliberately close to spoken Urdu, his metres are light, and his couplets often achieve force through understatement rather than ornament. He wrote about separation, decline, the self and the city with a directness that still reads as modern.

sections.heading: Later classicists
sections.text: Momin is known for intricate, compressed craft, Daagh Dehlvi for polished idiom and for training a generation of pupils in Lucknow and Hyderabad, and Bahadur Shah Zafar for ghazals shaped by exile and loss.

sections.heading: Influence
sections.text: Ghalib inherited and challenged this tradition; Firaq Gorakhpuri and later critics returned to Mir as a standard of natural expression. The Delhi school's preference for emotional truth over display remains a live critical idea in Urdu poetry.

topics.title: Faiz Ahmed Faiz
topics.summary: Faiz Ahmed Faiz was a twentieth-century Urdu poet and journalist who joined the classical ghazal's romantic vocabulary to political commitment, labour movements and anti-colonial hope. He is one of the most translated Urdu poets.

sections.heading: Life
sections.text: Born in 1911 in Sialkot district, he taught literature, edited journals, served in the army during the Second World War and was imprisoned in the 1950s for his political associations. Periods of exile in Beirut and Moscow broadened the geographical range of his work.

sections.heading: Poetic method
sections.text: Faiz keeps the radif, qafia and imagery of the classical ghazal but lets the beloved stand for a person, a homeland, a future or a collective hope at once. That ambiguity is why a single sher can be read as a love poem and as a political statement.

sections.heading: Collections
sections.text: Naqsh-e-Faryadi, Dast-e-Saba, Zindan Nama and Dast-e-Tah-e-Sang are among his best-known collections. Poems such as the ones beginning with the imagery of the blood-stained dawn and the imprisoned night are widely recited at public gatherings.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.text: He was associated with the Progressive Writers' Movement, and his verse has been set to music by many singers. Translations into English, Russian and other languages helped make the Urdu ghazal legible to readers outside South Asia.

topics.title: Modern Urdu poets
topics.summary: Twentieth-century Urdu poetry widened the tradition beyond the classical courts: progressive politics, existential irony, feminism, partition memory and plain modern speech all entered the ghazal and the nazm.

sections.heading: Josh and Firaq
sections.text: Josh Malihabadi is known for the energy, scale and rhetorical force of his nazms, while Firaq Gorakhpuri combined deep classical learning with a supple, conversational ghazal and influential criticism.

sections.heading: Progressives and film lyricists
sections.text: Sahir Ludhianvi, Kaifi Azmi, Ahmad Nadeem Qasmi and Majrooh Sultanpuri linked poetry to social criticism and to film song, which brought Urdu verse to a mass audience across South Asia.

sections.heading: Faraz, Shakir and their generation
sections.text: Ahmad Faraz used direct, romantic and dissenting diction that made him a popular public voice. Parveen Shakir introduced a distinctly feminine first person, playful imagery and a modern idiom that changed how the ghazal could speak.

sections.heading: Later voices
sections.text: Munir Niazi is remembered for haunting brevity, Nida Fazli for gentle philosophical lyricism, Jaun Elia for corrosive irony and candour, Iftikhar Arif for classical gravity, and Anwar Masood for humour and accessible narrative.

sections.heading: Contemporary scene
sections.text: Mushairas, television, recordings and social media now circulate Urdu poetry widely, and younger poets mix the ghazal with free verse, performance and code-switching between Urdu, Hindi and English.

topics.title: Mushaira and Urdu literary culture
topics.summary: A mushaira is a public gathering at which poets recite ghazals and nazms to a responsive audience. It is the principal performance institution of Urdu poetry and has shaped both how poems are written and how they are judged.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Poets are seated in an order of seniority and recite in rounds. The audience responds after individual couplets with appreciation, or asks for a repeat, so a sher that survives repeated public testing gains a life of its own independent of the printed page.

sections.heading: Recitation styles
sections.text: Tarannum is a melodic, measured recitation that can highlight the metre and the radif, while a plain reading emphasises argument and diction. Well-known poems are often recognised by the opening line, called the matla.

sections.heading: Institutions
sections.text: The takhallus, or pen name, conventionally appears in the final couplet, and the ustad-shagird relationship links a younger poet to a master who corrects metre and diction. Literary journals, radio, television and now online recordings extend the same culture beyond the hall.

sections.heading: Why it matters for reading
sections.text: Because a sher is designed to be heard once and understood immediately, compactness, sound and the placement of the refrain carry unusual weight. Reading a ghazal silently still benefits from imagining that audience.

topics.title: Poetic devices and scansion
topics.summary: Poetic devices are the repeatable techniques by which verse builds sound, emphasis and meaning. They include metre, rhyme, lineation, figurative language and patterns of repetition, and they work in both English and Urdu traditions even though the underlying prosodies differ.

sections.heading: Sound
sections.text: Rhyme, slant rhyme, assonance, consonance, alliteration and onomatopoeia organise the audible surface of a poem. In English, metre counts patterns of stress; in classical Urdu, aruz counts patterns of long and short syllables.

sections.heading: Line and syntax
sections.text: Enjambment lets a sentence run past a line break, while an end-stopped line closes at the break. A caesura places a pause inside a line. Both let a poet set grammar against rhythm so that meaning arrives slightly before or after the ear expects it.

sections.heading: Figurative language
sections.text: Metaphor, simile, metonymy, synecdoche, personification, symbol, allusion and irony compress comparison and argument. Imagery is not decoration: in most poems the pattern of images carries the claim that the literal statement only partially states.

sections.heading: Scansion in practice
sections.text: To scan an English line, mark stressed and unstressed syllables, name the recurring foot, and count the feet per line. To analyse an Urdu sher, identify the bahr, locate the qafia and radif, and check that every couplet keeps all three.

sections.heading: Structure and repetition
sections.text: Anaphora, refrain, parallelism, volta and stanza form create larger patterns across a poem. Repetition with variation is the most reliable way a poem builds pressure and then releases it.

topics.title: Comparing English and Urdu poetry
topics.summary: English and Urdu poetry share metaphor, imagery, refrain and performance, but they differ sharply in prosody, in the unit of composition, and in the relationship between poem and audience.

sections.heading: Prosody
sections.text: English metre is stress-based, counting accented syllables and feet. Classical Urdu metre is quantitative, counting long and short syllables in fixed aruz patterns. Rhyme in English usually falls at line ends; in the ghazal it is tied to a mandatory refrain structure.

sections.heading: Unit of composition
sections.text: An English lyric generally develops one continuous argument across stanzas. A ghazal is a sequence of autonomous couplets whose unity is tonal and formal rather than narrative, so a single sher can circulate independently for centuries.

sections.heading: Audience
sections.text: The mushaira gives Urdu poetry an immediate, vocal public that responds couplet by couplet. English poetry historically circulated through print and the silent reader, though spoken word and slam have recently revived performance.

sections.heading: Shared ground
sections.text: Both traditions use the beloved, the natural world, absence, time and mortality as central figures; both support mystical, political and ironic readings; and both were transformed by modern free verse and by translation.

sections.heading: Translation
sections.text: A sonnet loses its rhyme but can keep its turn; a ghazal loses its radif and its metre, so translators usually keep the autonomy of the couplet and add a note about the form. Neither tradition translates cleanly into the other, which is itself a useful critical insight.

topics.title: History of the atomic bomb
topics.summary: The atomic bomb is a weapon that releases energy by nuclear fission of uranium-235 or plutonium-239. It was developed by the United States Manhattan Project during the Second World War, first tested in July 1945, and used against Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945 - the only use of nuclear weapons in war.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: A fission bomb brings a sub-critical mass of fissile material rapidly into a super-critical configuration, either by firing one piece into another (a gun-type assembly, used for the uranium device) or by symmetrically compressing a plutonium core with conventional explosives (implosion). A chain reaction then splits nuclei and releases energy, neutrons and intense radiation within microseconds.

sections.heading: The Manhattan Project
sections.text: Begun in 1942 under the US Army Corps of Engineers and directed by J. Robert Oppenheimer at Los Alamos, the project combined theoretical physics, industrial-scale uranium enrichment at Oak Ridge, plutonium production at Hanford and bomb design at Los Alamos. It employed more than 100,000 people and cost roughly two billion dollars in 1945 money.

sections.heading: 1945: test and use
sections.text: The first nuclear test, Trinity, took place on 16 July 1945 in New Mexico. On 6 August 1945 a uranium gun-type bomb was dropped on Hiroshima, and on 9 August a plutonium implosion bomb was dropped on Nagasaki. Japan announced its surrender on 15 August. Casualty estimates remain debated, but well over 100,000 people died in the two cities by the end of 1945, most of them civilians.

sections.heading: Aftermath and the nuclear age
sections.text: The Soviet Union tested a bomb in 1949, ending the American monopoly, and the hydrogen bomb followed in the 1950s. The doctrine of mutually assured destruction shaped Cold War strategy, while the 1968 Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons and later test-ban and arms-reduction agreements tried to limit spread and stockpiles.

sections.heading: Why the history is contested
sections.text: Historians disagree about the weight to give to ending the war quickly, to the demonstration of power before the Soviet Union, and to the moral cost of targeting cities. The decision is one of the most studied problems in modern history, so a careful answer presents the arguments and the evidence rather than a single settled verdict.

sections.heading: Common confusions
sections.text: An atomic (fission) bomb is not a hydrogen (thermonuclear fusion) bomb; the latter is far more powerful and uses a fission device as a trigger. A nuclear reactor is not a bomb: reactor fuel is not enriched to weapons grade and the geometry cannot produce a nuclear explosion. 'The Making of the Atomic Bomb' is a 1986 history book by Richard Rhodes, not the event itself.

topics.example: A useful exam framing: cause (wartime research and fear of a German bomb), mechanism (fission), event (Trinity, Hiroshima, Nagasaki), consequence (Cold War deterrence and non-proliferation), and evaluation (the unresolved moral debate).

topics.title: Stopping a stuck process
topics.summary: To stop a stuck process, first send it a graceful termination signal, then escalate to a forced kill only if it ignores that signal. On Linux and macOS use kill with the process ID, on Windows use taskkill or Stop-Process, and never kill a process you cannot identify.

sections.heading: Find the process ID
sections.text: On Linux or macOS run ps aux | grep <name>, pgrep -fl <name>, or top / htop to find the PID. On Windows use Task Manager, tasklist, or Get-Process in PowerShell. Confirm the exact command line before acting, because similarly named processes may belong to the operating system.

sections.heading: Ask it to stop first
sections.text: On Unix-like systems kill <PID> sends SIGTERM (signal 15), which lets the program save state, close files and shut down cleanly. Many applications also have a proper quit command or a service manager: sudo systemctl stop <service> is preferable to killing a managed daemon.

sections.heading: Escalate only when needed
sections.text: If the process ignores SIGTERM, kill -9 <PID> sends SIGKILL, which the kernel enforces and the program cannot catch or clean up after. That can leave lock files, corrupted writes or orphaned child processes, so treat it as a last resort. On PowerShell use Stop-Process -Id <PID> -Force; in cmd use taskkill /PID <PID> /F.

sections.heading: If it is a Python program
sections.text: A pure-Python loop can be interrupted with Ctrl+C in its terminal, which raises KeyboardInterrupt; handle that exception to shut down cleanly. A process blocked in a C extension or a system call may not respond until the call returns. For long-running jobs, build in a timeout, a cancellation flag or a signal handler.

sections.heading: Prevention
sections.text: Wrap workers in supervising tools (systemd, supervisor, Docker restart policies, or a job queue with timeouts), log a heartbeat, and use process groups so children are terminated with their parent. A stuck process is usually a symptom of a missing timeout or an unbounded wait.

topics.example: pgrep -fl python; kill 12345; sleep 2; pgrep -fl python && kill -9 12345  # graceful first, forced only if still alive
topics.code:
# Graceful shutdown inside a Python worker
import signal, sys

def stop(signum, frame):
    print('shutting down cleanly')
    sys.exit(0)

signal.signal(signal.SIGTERM, stop)

topics.title: Capital cities and why they are confusing
aliases: why is the capital not the largest city
topics.summary: A capital is the city that formally hosts a country's central government. It is often not the largest city: Australia has Canberra rather than Sydney, Canada has Ottawa rather than Toronto, and Turkey has Ankara rather than Istanbul.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.text: Capital status is a legal and political designation, not a measure of population or economic weight. Some countries name it in their constitution, others by ordinary law, and a few - such as South Africa - split the executive, legislative and judicial capitals between different cities.

sections.heading: Why the largest city is usually not the capital
sections.text: Capitals are sometimes chosen deliberately to balance rival regions, to move government away from a dominant commercial centre, or to occupy a purpose-built planned city. Canberra, Brasília, Abuja, Islamabad and Naypyidaw are all examples of planned or relocated capitals.

sections.heading: How to answer a capital question accurately
sections.text: Name the country's current official capital first. Then, if useful, mention any historical capital, the largest city, and any disputed status. Never answer with a paragraph about a different country simply because a search result happened to mention your country.

sections.heading: Disputed and changing cases
sections.text: Jerusalem's status is disputed internationally, Bolivia has a constitutional capital and a separate seat of government, and Kazakhstan briefly renamed Astana to Nur-Sultan. A careful answer states the convention and the date rather than pretending there is no ambiguity.

topics.example: Japan -> Tokyo (not Kyoto, the imperial capital until 1868). France -> Paris. Pakistan -> Islamabad (not Karachi).
